topic.name: The Chain Rule for Total Derivatives

question.text:
Consider the functions $\mathbf y: \mathbb R^3\to \mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^2,$ defined by
\[
\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1x_2x_3 \\ x_1+x_2+x_3 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 + y_2 \\ y_1y_2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
What is 
$\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at 
$\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.freeAnswerChoice:
$\left.\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))\right|_{\mathbf x_0}= \:\:$ [ answer: 7; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: 4; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: 3; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ]
$42$ [ answer: 24; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] $18$
question.explanation:
Using the chain rule, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}. \]

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y_2} \\ \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y_2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_1}(y_1 + y_2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_2}(y_1 + y_2) \\ \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_1}(y_1y_2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_2}(y_1y_2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ y_2 & y_1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Evaluating at $\mathbf{y}_0 = \mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \\ 1+2+3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. \]
  • The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_3} \\ \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_2} & \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_3} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(x_1x_2x_3) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_1x_2x_3) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_3}(x_1x_2x_3) \\ \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(x_1+x_2+x_3) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_1+x_2+x_3) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_3}(x_1+x_2+x_3) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} x_2x_3 & x_1x_3 & x_1x_2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Evaluating at $\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} &= \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{7}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{4}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{3}} \\ 42 & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{24}} & 18 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the functions $\mathbf y: \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^2,$ defined by
\[
\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_1^2+x_2^2\right) \\ x_1 + x_2 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad 
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1y_2 \\ y_1^2 + y_2^2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
What is 
$\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at 
$\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.freeAnswerChoice:
$\left.\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))\right|_{\mathbf x_0}= \:\:$ [ answer: 2; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; buttons: frac; ] [ answer: 6; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; buttons: frac; ]
$4$ [ answer: 12; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; buttons: frac; ]
question.explanation:
Using the chain rule, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}. \]

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y_2} \\ \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y_2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_1}(y_1y_2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_2}(y_1y_2) \\ \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_1}(y_1^2 + y_2^2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_2}(y_1^2 + y_2^2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} y_2 & y_1 \\ 2y_1 & 2y_2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Evaluating at $\mathbf{y}_0 = \mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}_0) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2}\left(0^2 + 2^2\right) \\ 0 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]
  • The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_2} \\ \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_1^2+x_2^2\right)\right) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_1^2+x_2^2\right)\right) \\ \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1}(x_1 + x_2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}(x_1 + x_2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Evaluating at $\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} &= \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{2}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{6}} \\ 4 & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{12}} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the functions $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{y},$ where $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^2,$ and the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are given by
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1, \, -1, \, 3]^T?$
question.freeAnswerChoice:
$\left.\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))\right|_{\mathbf x_0}= \:\:$ [ answer: 4; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: -2; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: 6; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ]
$-7$ [ answer: -4; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] $-3$
question.explanation:
Using the chain rule, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}. \]

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, \[\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.\]

  • The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, \[\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.\]

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) &= \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{4}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{-2}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{6}} \\ -7 & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{-4}} & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
For $\mathbf x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z\in\mathbb R^2,$ consider the following functions:

\begin{align*} & \mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \quad \text{where} \quad \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] & \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1^2 + y_2 \\ y_2^2 - y_1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] & \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{z} \quad \text{where} \quad \mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*} What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.explanation:
Using the chain rule, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}. \]

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{C}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} = \mathbf{C}. \]

  • The function $\mathbf{z}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_2} \\ \dfrac{\partial z_2}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial z_2}{\partial y_2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2y_1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2y_2 \end{bmatrix}. \] Evaluating at $\mathbf{y}_0 = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 2(-1) & 1 \\ -1 & 2(0) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, \[ \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}. \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} &= \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} \bigg|_{\mathbf{z}_0} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \bigg|_{\mathbf{y}_0} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_0} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
